{{Short description|Equation known for chaotic behavior}}
{{technical|date=May 2025}}[[File:Kuramoto–Sivashinsky spatiotemporal evolution.png|thumb|250px|A spatiotemporal plot of a simulation of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation]]

In [[mathematics]], the '''Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation''' (also called the '''KS equation''') is a [[partial differential equation]] used to model complex patterns and chaotic behavior in physical systems. It is one of the simplest PDEs known to exhibit [[Chaos theory|chaos]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pathak |first1=Jaideep |last2=Hunt |first2=Brian |last3=Girvan |first3=Michelle |last4=Lu |first4=Zhixin |last5=Ott |first5=Edward |date=2018 |title=Model-Free Prediction of Large Spatiotemporally Chaotic Systems from Data: A Reservoir Computing Approach |journal=Physical Review Letters |language=en |volume=120 |issue=2 |article-number=024102 |bibcode=2018PhRvL.120b4102P |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.120.024102 |issn=0031-9007 |pmid=29376715 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Vlachas |first1=P.R. |last2=Pathak |first2=J. |last3=Hunt |first3=B.R. |last4=Sapsis |first4=T.P. |last5=Girvan |first5=M. |last6=Ott |first6=E. |last7=Koumoutsakos |first7=P. |date=2020-03-21 |title=Backpropagation algorithms and Reservoir Computing in Recurrent Neural Networks for the forecasting of complex spatiotemporal dynamics |journal=Neural Networks |volume=126 |pages=191–217 |arxiv=1910.05266 |doi=10.1016/j.neunet.2020.02.016 |issn=0893-6080 |pmid=32248008 |bibcode=2020NN....126..191V |s2cid=211146609 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The fourth-order equation was first derived in the late 1970s by [[Yoshiki Kuramoto]] and [[Gregory Sivashinsky]] to describe the instabilities of a [[Laminar flow|laminar]] flame front.<ref name="Kuramoto19783">{{cite journal |last1=Kuramoto |first1=Yoshiki |year=1978 |title=Diffusion-Induced Chaos in Reaction Systems |journal=Progress of Theoretical Physics Supplement |volume=64 |pages=346–367 |bibcode=1978PThPS..64..346K |doi=10.1143/PTPS.64.346 |issn=0375-9687 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Sivashinsky19773">{{cite journal |last1=Sivashinsky |first1=G.I. |year=1977 |title=Nonlinear analysis of hydrodynamic instability in laminar flames—I. Derivation of basic equations |journal=Acta Astronautica |volume=4 |issue=11–12 |pages=1177–1206 |bibcode=1977AcAau...4.1177S |doi=10.1016/0094-5765(77)90096-0 |issn=0094-5765}}</ref><ref name="Sivashinsky19803">{{cite journal |last1=Sivashinsky |first1=G. I. |year=1980 |title=On Flame Propagation Under Conditions of Stoichiometry |journal=SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics |volume=39 |issue=1 |pages=67–82 |doi=10.1137/0139007 |issn=0036-1399}}</ref> It has since been found to apply to other systems, such as the flow of a thin liquid film down an inclined plane<ref>{{cite book |last1=Homsy |first1=G. M. |title=Nonlinear Wave Motion |publisher=American Mathematical Society |year=1974 |editor=Newell, A. |series=Lectures in Applied Mathematics |volume=15 |location=Providence |pages=191–194 |chapter=Model equations for wavy viscous film flow |bibcode=1974LApM...15.....N}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nepomnyashchii |first1=A. A. |date=1975 |title=Stability of wavy conditions in a film flowing down an inclined plane |journal=Fluid Dynamics |volume=9 |issue=3 |pages=354–359 |doi=10.1007/BF01025515}}</ref> and trapped-ion instability in plasmas.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Laquey |first1=R. E. |last2=Mahajan |first2=S. M. |last3=Rutherford |first3=P. H. |last4=Tang |first4=W. M. |date=1975 |title=Nonlinear Saturation of the Trapped-Ion Mode |url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc879108/ |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=34 |issue=7 |pages=391–394 |bibcode=1975PhRvL..34..391L |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.34.391}}</ref>

==Definition==
The 1d version of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation is
<math display="block">\partial_t u + \partial_x^2 u + \partial_x^4 u + \tfrac{1}{2} (\partial_x u)^2 = 0</math>
An alternate form is
<math display="block">\partial_t v + \partial_x^2 v + \partial_x^4 v + v \, \partial_x v = 0</math>
obtained by differentiating with respect to <math>x</math> and substituting <math>v = \partial_x u</math>. This is the form used in [[fluid dynamics]] applications.<ref name="KalogirouKeaveny2015">{{cite journal|last1=Kalogirou|first1=A.|last2=Keaveny|first2=E. E.|last3=Papageorgiou|first3=D. T.|title=An in-depth numerical study of the two-dimensional Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences|volume=471|issue=2179|year=2015|article-number=20140932|issn=1364-5021|doi=10.1098/rspa.2014.0932|pmid=26345218 | pmc=4528647|bibcode=2015RSPSA.47140932K }}</ref>

The Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation can also be generalized to higher dimensions. In spatially periodic domains, one possibility is
<math display="block">\partial_t u + \Delta u + \Delta^2 u + \tfrac{1}{2} \left|\nabla u\right|^2 = 0,</math>
where <math>\Delta</math> is the [[Laplace operator]], and <math>\Delta^2</math> is the [[biharmonic equation|biharmonic operator]].

==Properties==
The [[Cauchy problem]] for the 1d Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation is [[Well-posed problem|well-posed]] in the sense of Hadamard—that is, for given initial data <math>u(x, 0)</math>, there exists a unique solution <math>u(x, 0 \leq t < \infty)</math> that depends continuously on the initial data.<ref name="Tadmor1986">{{cite journal|last1=Tadmor|first1=Eitan|title=The Well-Posedness of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky Equation|journal=SIAM Journal on Mathematical Analysis|volume=17|issue=4|year=1986|pages=884–893|issn=0036-1410|doi=10.1137/0517063|hdl=1903/8432 |hdl-access=free}}</ref>

The 1d Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation possesses [[Galilean invariance]]—that is, if <math>u(x,t)</math> is a solution, then so is <math>u(x{-}ct, t) - c</math>, where <math>c</math> is an arbitrary constant.<ref name="CvitanovićDavidchack2010">{{cite journal|last1=Cvitanović|first1=Predrag|last2=Davidchack|first2=Ruslan L.|last3=Siminos|first3=Evangelos|author-link=Predrag Cvitanović|title=On the State Space Geometry of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky Flow in a Periodic Domain|journal=SIAM Journal on Applied Dynamical Systems|volume=9|issue=1|year=2010|pages=1–33|issn=1536-0040|doi=10.1137/070705623|arxiv=0709.2944 |bibcode=2010SJADS...9....1C |s2cid=17048798 }}</ref> Physically, since <math>u</math> is a velocity, this change of variable describes a transformation into a frame that is moving with constant [[relative velocity]] <math>c</math>. On a periodic domain, the equation also has a [[reflection symmetry]]: if <math>u(x,t)</math> is a solution, then <math>-u(-x, t)</math> is also a solution.<ref name="CvitanovićDavidchack2010"/>

==Solutions==
[[File:KuramotoSivashinskyRPO1.gif|thumb|A converged relative periodic orbit for the KS equation with periodic boundary conditions for a domain size <math>L=35</math>. After some time the system returns to its initial state, only translated slightly (~4 units) to the left. This particular solution has three unstable directions and three marginal directions.]]
Solutions of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation possess rich dynamical characteristics.<ref name="CvitanovićDavidchack2010"/><ref name="Michelson1986">{{cite journal|last1=Michelson|first1=Daniel|title=Steady solutions of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation|journal=Physica D: Nonlinear Phenomena|volume=19|issue=1|year=1986|pages=89–111|issn=0167-2789|doi=10.1016/0167-2789(86)90055-2|bibcode=1986PhyD...19...89M }}</ref><ref name="Papageorgiou1991">{{Citation|last1 = Papageorgiou|first1 = D.T.|last2 = Smyrlis|first2 = Y.S.|year = 1991|title = The route to chaos for the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation|journal = Theoret. Comput. Fluid Dynamics|volume = 3| issue=1 |pages = 15–42|doi = 10.1007/BF00271514| bibcode=1991ThCFD...3...15P | hdl=2060/19910004329 | s2cid=116955014 |issn = 1432-2250|hdl-access = free}}</ref> Considered on a periodic domain <math>0 \leq x \leq L </math>, the dynamics undergoes a series of [[Bifurcation theory|bifurcation]]s as the domain size <math>L</math> is increased, culminating in the onset of [[Chaos theory|chaotic]] behavior. Depending on the value of <math>L</math>, solutions may include equilibria, relative equilibria, and [[traveling waves]]—all of which typically become dynamically unstable as <math>L</math> is increased. In particular, the transition to chaos occurs by a cascade of [[period-doubling bifurcation]]s.<ref name="Papageorgiou1991"/>

==Modified Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation==
===Dispersive Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equations===
A third-order derivative term representing dispersion of wavenumbers are often encountered in many applications. The dispersively modified Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation, which is often called as the '''Kawahara equation''',<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Topper|first1=J.|last2=Kawahara|first2=T.|title=Approximate equations for long nonlinear waves on a viscous fluid|journal=Journal of the Physical Society of Japan|volume=44|issue=2|year=1978|pages=663–666|doi=10.1143/JPSJ.44.2003|doi-access=free|bibcode=1978JPSJ...44.2003T }}</ref> is given by<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Chang|first1=H. C.|last2=Demekhin|first2=E. A. |last3=Kopelevich|first3=D. I.|title=Laminarizing effects of dispersion in an active-dissipative nonlinear medium|journal=Physica D: Nonlinear Phenomena|volume=63|issue=3–4|year=1993|pages=299–320|issn=1872-8022|doi=10.1016/0167-2789(93)90113-F|bibcode=1993PhyD...63..299C }}</ref>

<math display="block">\partial_t u + \partial_x^2 u + \delta_3 \partial_x^3 u + \partial_x^4 u + u \, \partial_x u = 0</math>

where <math>\delta_3</math> is real parameter. A fifth-order derivative term is also often included, which is the modified Kawahara equation and is given by<ref>Akrivis, G., Papageorgiou, D. T., & Smyrlis, Y. S. (2012). Computational study of the dispersively modified Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation. SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing, 34(2), A792-A813.</ref>

<math display="block">\partial_t u + \partial_x^2 u + \delta_3 \partial_x^3 u + \partial_x^4 u + \delta_5 \partial_x^5 u + u \, \partial_x u = 0.</math>

===Sixth-order equations===
Three forms of the sixth-order Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equations are encountered in applications involving [[Tricritical point|tricritical points]], which are given by<ref name="RD">{{cite journal|last1=Rajamanickam|first1=P.|last2=Daou|first2=J.|title=Tricritical point as a crossover between type-Is and type-IIs bifurcations|journal=Progress in Scale Modeling |volume=4|issue=1|year=2023|page=2|issn=2693-969X|doi=10.13023/psmij.2023.04-01-02|doi-access=free}}</ref>

<math display="block">\begin{alignat}{7}
\partial_t u &{}+{}& q \partial_x^2 u &{}+{}& \partial_x^4 u &{}-{}& \partial_x^6 u &{}+{}& u \, \partial_x u &{}={}& 0, &\quad q>0,\\[1ex]
\partial_t u &{}+{}&   \partial_x^2 u &{} {}&                &{}-{}& \partial_x^6 u &{}+{}& u \, \partial_x u &{}={}& 0, \\[1ex]
\partial_t u &{}+{}& q \partial_x^2 u &{}-{}& \partial_x^4 u &{}-{}& \partial_x^6 u &{}+{}& u \, \partial_x u &{}={}& 0, &\quad q>-\tfrac{1}{4}
\end{alignat}</math>

in which the last equation is referred to as the '''Nikolaevsky equation''', named after V. N. Nikolaevsky who introduced the equation in 1989,<ref>Nikolaevskii, V. N. (1989). Dynamics of viscoelastic media with internal oscillators. In Recent Advances in Engineering Science: A Symposium dedicated to A. Cemal Eringen June 20–22, 1988, Berkeley, California (pp. 210-221). Berlin, Heidelberg: Springer Berlin Heidelberg.</ref><ref>Tribelsky, M. I., & Tsuboi, K. (1996). New scenario for transition to turbulence?. Physical review letters, 76(10), 1631.</ref><ref>Matthews, P. C., & Cox, S. M. (2000). One-dimensional pattern formation with Galilean invariance near a stationary bifurcation. Physical Review E, 62(2), R1473.</ref> whereas the first two equations has been introduced by P. Rajamanickam and J. Daou in the context of transitions near tricritical points,{{r|RD}} i.e., change in the sign of the fourth derivative term with the plus sign approaching a Kuramoto–Sivashinsky type and the minus sign approaching a [[Ginzburg–Landau equation|Ginzburg–Landau type]].

==Applications==
Applications of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation extend beyond its original context of flame propagation and [[reaction–diffusion system]]s. These additional applications include [[Pipe flow|flows in pipes]] and at interfaces, [[Plasma (physics)|plasma]]s, [[chemical reaction]] dynamics, and models of [[Sputtering|ion-sputtered]] surfaces.<ref name="KalogirouKeaveny2015"/><ref name="CuernoBarabási1995">{{cite journal|last1=Cuerno|first1=Rodolfo|last2=Barabási|first2=Albert-László|title=Dynamic Scaling of Ion-Sputtered Surfaces|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=74|issue=23|year=1995|pages=4746–4749|issn=0031-9007|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.74.4746 |pmid=10058588 | arxiv=cond-mat/9411083 |bibcode=1995PhRvL..74.4746C |s2cid=18148655 }}</ref>
